name: ucg (UniversalCodeGrep)
workload: Recursive search of a built Linux kernel source tree for the whole-word regex [A-Z]+_SUSPEND, restricted to C source files (gitignore handling disabled for ripgrep, --include filters for grep, ucg --type=cc).
claimed_speedup: ripgrep 0.8.0 README: ucg 0.163s vs GNU grep 0.611s (about 3.7x faster, derived from page data) on the same corpus; ripgrep itself 0.079s, so ucg is about 2x slower than ripgrep. ucg returned 390 matching lines against 404 for grep and ripgrep.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for ucg or GNU grep (only 'ripgrep was compiled with SIMD enabled'); commands: ucg --type=cc -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND' versus egrep -R -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'.
hardware: Intel i7-6900K 3.2 GHz (per the ripgrep 0.8.0 README, kernel tree built with make defconfig && make -j8)
stars_or_usage: 144 stars; packaged for Fedora (Copr), Arch (AUR) and Homebrew core
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-only (copyleft). Uses PCRE2 with JIT, a multithreaded directory walker and hand-rolled SSE2/SSE4.2 scan loops chosen at load time. Does not read .gitignore; it relies on a built-in per-language file whitelist. Search patterns are PCRE only. Command-line compatible with ack, partly with ag and grep.
caveats: The benchmark was run by the author of the competing tool ripgrep (third party to ucg, but a competitor), and the README only gives the CPU and the ripgrep build; ucg and GNU grep versions and compiler flags are not in the README (the linked blog post that probably lists them was not reachable: blog.burntsushi.net and burntsushi.net returned ENOTFOUND). ucg's own README (https://github.com/gvansickle/ucg, opened) has a first-party table: Boost 1.58.0 source, pattern '#include\s+.*', Fedora 25, average of 10 runs, ucg 0.3.0 0.228973s, ripgrep 0.2.9 0.167586s, ag 0.32.0 2.29074s (about 10x slower than ucg, derived), GNU grep 2.26 0.370082s (about 1.6x slower, derived); its 'Num Diff Chars' column shows ucg output differs from grep's by 189 characters and 9511 matched lines against 9509. That table is first-party (tier C on its own), has no CPU or compiler flags, and ripgrep wins it. The numbers are from 2016-2018 era versions; ucg is slower than ripgrep in both sources, and the ripgrep table notes ucg handles symlinks differently (gvansickle/ucg issue 106, closed 2017, 390 versus 404 lines was a traversal difference). Recent repo commits (2026-09-14) are CI, m4 and perf-comparison script changes; the last source-code change found was 2024-12-28. ucg's test suite (tests/performance_tests.at and tests/benchmark_progs.csv) is public and can regenerate the comparison, but no recent numbers are published.
found_via: seed-record pass: ripgrep 0.8.0 README benchmark table (https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/blob/0.8.0/README.md) plus the ucg README

name: merve (nodejs CommonJS export lexer)
baseline: cjs-module-lexer (the JS/WebAssembly lexer previously bundled in Node.js core)
workload: Node.js benchmark esm/import-cjs.js: ESM import() of a CommonJS fixture (typescript.js, 2000+ exports), cold (one first import) and warm (ten imports), comparing a Node build using merve against one using cjs-module-lexer.
claimed_speedup: Node PR 61456 body: 'the new cjs module lexer is 25% faster for cold importing cjs files'. Benchmark CI run 1784 in the PR: esm/import-cjs.js type='cold' +26.83 % (accuracy +/-0.58%, *** confidence), type='warm' +11.95 % (+/-0.14%, ***).
stars_or_usage: 63 stars; replaced cjs-module-lexer in Node.js core (PR 61456 merged 2026-01-28, shipped in v24.14.0 LTS and v25.6.1)
tradeoffs: Zero-copy export names via std::string_view, single pass without backtracking, consteval lookup tables, optional simdutf for escape detection (off by default, Node enables it). Ships a C API and Rust bindings, no dependencies. Detection behavior must match the frozen cjs-module-lexer patterns; error handling returns std::optional. The old lexer was JS plus WebAssembly, so the swap also removes wasm instantiation from the cold path.
caveats: The numbers come from the PR author's own Node Benchmark CI run (the author, anonrig, also wrote merve); the CI console at ci.nodejs.org was not reachable (ENOTFOUND), so CPU, compiler and flags are unknown. The benchmark is end-to-end import() of typescript.js, which includes reading, wrapping and compiling the file, so the lexer-only speedup is not isolated; it compares whole Node builds that also changed the binding (native C++ instead of JS calling wasm), and the cold row includes wasm initialization for the baseline. The merve README gives no numbers and the optional MERVE_BENCHMARKS target (default OFF) was not found with sources in the tests directory or repo root. Post-merge regressions were reported: nodejs/node issue 62212 (SIGSEGV importing a large webpack bundle, merve regression in v24.14.0), issue 63323 (crash in cjs_lexer::Parse, fixed by PR 63885) and nodejs/merve issue 49 (Vite/browser import * breakage). Rows quoted from the PR page via a summarizing fetch; the esm/detect-esm-syntax rows (+1.47%, +0.64%) are within noise-level gains.
found_via: seed-record pass: nodejs/merve README (no numbers), then PR build,deps: replace cjs-module-lexer with merve (https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/61456) found via the Node pull request list for 'merve'
